419.history: The silver town lies in the far east of the hills on a shelf of the valley under the moor, an hour's walk from the old walls at Dùn ìseal. Its guild, Comann an Airgid, held its seam under a compact that Ùna locked in the guild chest in the first half-century, and the surveyors who came for its ledgers were turned back at the adit. The guild sent its bar to the sea by Seann Bhral rather than the Company's quays, paid for the mark in silver, refused Martha Gale's partnership in the sixty-seventh year by a count of hands in its hall, and in the years before the war bought rifles from the raiders of the eastern waters and entered them in its ledger as refining tools. In the rising its riflemen took Dùn ìseal and cleared the east of human arms. The seam is silver near the great vein but not of it. Catrìona nic Eachainn, a refiner of the guild, died there an old woman in the hundred and fourth year, and Ùna nic Choinnich headed the guild into her eightieth winter.
419.known_for: the guild compact and its riflemen

110.history: The greatest harbour of the south-eastern coast, where the oyster-beds lie in the shallows, loaded the silver town's bar for the coasting boats as it had since An Aois Naomh. From the forty-fourth year the guild sent all its silver south by this road, eighteen miles down the valley, and paid the custodians of the port in silver by the Muileann chiar weight on every bar. When a collier burned off the coast the Company's agents said at its quays that the guild had paid the raiders to do it; the charge was never proved. Torcall's crews built its new quay in the first years of the strangers. Its harbour is the largest of that coast, and in the war its custodians turned the Company's coasters away without a shot fired.
110.known_for: the silver road to the sea

258.history: The red ford-town on the north-eastern cape kept a fire on a shelf of the headland for its boats long before any roll, and when the humans asked for a tower there the custodian went round every hearth to ask leave, which took eleven days. The mason Tormod mac Pheadair built the tower and kept it, and began in it the first daybook of the five lights, so plain that the Company's clerk who read it called its keeper civil but of no assistance. On a night of gale in the forty-sixth year the light brought four boats of Àth dhearg home off the long lines. In the war its light went dark with the others of the south, and was lit again at the truce. A clerk of A' Chompanaidh rode up the coast road in the dark days of Dubhlas to ask to see the daybook about the burning of a collier, and went away with nothing.

476.history: The walled city of white stone on the far western coast was a Dia-thìreach town until the human families of the northern concession made it their market in the fiftieth year. Its Mission kept a chapel and, in the fever years, a hospital where Dia-thìrich and human sick lay side by side for the first time because there was no longer room to keep them apart; Hannah Webb nursed in its wards. In the war it shut its gates, raised a militia that went nowhere, and its magistrate asked both sides to be left alone. Its harbour officer rode south with his town's keys at the end. Obadiah Renn, the minister of its Mission, sat with Hannah Webb in the chapel over her vigil, and wrote of it to the Mission's house at Cathair dhearg.
476.known_for: the concession's market and the shared wards

143.history: The great harbour under the north-western headland took in the first human fishing families of the concession in the fifty-first year, the first humans to fish the island's waters for their own living. Tobacco grew on the concession farms behind it. Manannan's priests kept the grey night on its quay, and Ruth Pallant, who taught Hannah Webb the night watch, lived near it. Gorta Baile chrom struck it hard. At the close of the age its harbour officer carried the town's chest of keys two days south to Cuan shean. Its harbour lies under the beacon of Taigh-solais Baile chrom, and in the hunger years it sent what boats it had south along the coast for grain.

371.history: The river port of the north-west opened a school of its own in the fifty-second year in answer to the Mission's, and taught the old reckoning, the rolls and the names of the hills; the next year the Mission complained in writing that the children who came to its school from Inis bhàn already knew how to argue, and the custodians kept the complaint as a testimonial. In the season of the hawk sermons its priests of the hawk sat down for the first time with the last teachers of the druid disputations. Its barges run down to Ros gheal on the coast, and its roll kept the names of the children who went to the custodians' school beside the names of those who went to the Mission's.
371.known_for: its school, and the Mission's complaint
